message.content:
The number of distinct positions that can arise in a standard game of chess is astronomically large – on the order of **10⁴³**.  

This figure, often called the *Shannon number*, is an estimate of the size of the game‑tree complexity of chess. It counts only *legal* positions that could actually occur during play, taking into account all the rules (e.g., no two kings in check, correct castling rights, en‑passant possibilities, etc.).

If you ignore the rules and simply count every way to place the 32 pieces (16 white + 16 black) on the 64 squares, the number jumps to roughly **10⁴⁶**.  

So:

| Context | Rough estimate |
|---------|----------------|
| Legal positions (the “real” game‑tree) | ≈ 10⁴³ |
| All possible piece placements (ignoring legality) | ≈ 10⁴⁶ |

These numbers are widely cited in chess literature and give a sense of how vast the combinatorial space of the game is.
